facts.fact: The 2026 World Cup will be the first to feature 48 teams, up from 32 in previous tournaments.
Brazil has won the most World Cups (5), followed by Germany and Italy with 4 each.
For the first time ever, 3 nations co-host: USA, Canada, and Mexico.
MetLife Stadium (82,500 seats) will host the 2026 World Cup Final on July 19.
Lionel Messi holds the record for most World Cup appearances with 26 matches.
The fastest goal in World Cup history was scored by Hakan Şükür in just 11 seconds (2002).
The 1950 final at Maracanã drew an estimated 199,854 fans — the largest crowd ever.
Estadio Azteca becomes the first stadium to host World Cup matches in 3 different editions (1970, 1986, 2026).
Marta of Brazil is the all-time leading World Cup scorer across men's and women's tournaments with 17 goals.
The 2026 tournament will feature 104 matches — the most in World Cup history.
Uruguay won the first ever World Cup in 1930, defeating Argentina 4-2 in the final.
The World Cup trophy was stolen in 1966 and found by a dog named Pickles under a bush in London.
Just Fontaine scored 13 goals in a single World Cup (1958) — a record that still stands.
SoFi Stadium cost $5.5 billion to build, making it the most expensive stadium in the world.
The 2026 World Cup lasts 39 days, from June 11 to July 19, 2026.
Germany's Miroslav Klose is the all-time men's World Cup top scorer with 16 goals.
Canada will host World Cup matches for the first time in the nation's history.
Only two nations have won back-to-back World Cups: Italy (1934, 1938) and Brazil (1958, 1962).
AT&T Stadium features the world's largest HD video board, stretching 72 feet tall.
Pelé is the youngest World Cup winner at 17 years old, triumphing with Brazil in 1958.
The highest-scoring World Cup match was Austria 7-5 Switzerland in 1954 — 12 goals total.
The Round of 32 is a brand new knockout stage, expanding from the previous Round of 16 format.
India qualified for the 1950 World Cup but withdrew because they weren't allowed to play barefoot.
Matches will span 4 time zones across North America, from Pacific to Eastern.
